headline: Alabama’s Proposed Data Centers Could Dwarf Home Energy Use, Sparking Bill Shock Fears
deck: At least a dozen data centers planned for Alabama would consume more electricity than all state homes combined, yet the utility insists bills won’t rise.
body: Alabama is barreling toward an energy crisis disguised as economic progress. An Inside Climate News analysis reveals that at least a dozen proposed data centers, if built to full capacity, would outstrip the electricity demand of every home in the state. The sheer scale of these facilities—some exceeding the power needs of entire counties—has ignited alarm among residents already saddled with the nation’s highest average residential electricity bills. Alabama Power, the state’s dominant utility, insists the projects won’t inflate customer costs, a claim that grows harder to swallow with each new megawatt request.

Alabama Power’s monopoly grip on much of the state gives it unchecked authority over power pricing and distribution. The utility’s advertisements promise that data centers won’t drive up bills, urging customers to ‘trust the process.’ But trust is a scarce commodity in a state where residents already pay more for electricity than anywhere else in the country. Shannon Vanden Heuvel, a local marketing designer, cuts through the corporate messaging with brutal honesty. ‘I don’t believe a word they say,’ she said. Her skepticism reflects a broader distrust in an energy system where the utility’s word seems to carry more weight than the public’s wallets.

The tension isn’t just hypothetical. Alabama Power’s service area already forces households to shoulder some of the steepest power costs in the U.S., a burden that predates the data center boom. Now, with a dozen facilities poised to demand enough electricity to render residential consumption trivial, the math becomes impossible to ignore. Even if the data centers pay for their power, the infrastructure upgrades and grid strain will ripple through the system—costs that rarely stay neatly contained.

State lawmakers have attempted to claw back some control. SB 270, enacted this year, tasks the Public Service Commission (PSC) with vetting every data center contract to ensure it serves the ‘public interest.’ The law demands scrutiny of whether pricing and terms could actually lower costs for other customers or at least ensure data center operators—not ratepayers—foot the bill for incremental expenses. Yet the PSC’s interpretation of ‘public interest’ remains the final, untested variable in this high-stakes equation.

The law’s requirements are clear on paper, but enforcement is murky. SB 270 forces the PSC to weigh two competing priorities: attracting corporate investment and protecting residents from financial ruin. Analysts note that the commission has historically deferred to utility companies, leaving little precedent for aggressive pushback. The law’s passage may have been a step forward, but whether it translates into real protection is another question entirely.

For now, the data center developers march ahead, their promises of job creation and economic growth drowning out the chorus of ratepayer unease. Alabama Power’s advertisements continue to blanket the airwaves, repeating the mantra that bills won’t rise. Yet the state’s own data tells a different story: residential electricity costs are already unsustainable, and the proposed projects could turn a bad situation catastrophic. The question isn’t whether the grid can handle the load—it’s who will pay for the damage.

The PSC’s role as the final arbiter under SB 270 places an outsized burden on its commissioners. Their decisions will shape Alabama’s energy future, determining whether the state’s residents become the unwitting underwriters of a corporate power grab. With the public watching and the stakes higher than ever, the commission’s next moves could either defuse a brewing crisis or confirm residents’ worst fears about who truly benefits from their sky-high bills.
